title: Industrial Expansion Joints | Design Practice
subtitle: Bellows, flanges, piping components and mechanical design verification
overview: During industrial mechanical design work at Enetaf Sane Co. (Jan 2022–Jul 2023), worked on expansion joints, bellows, flanges and piping-related equipment. The focus was translating service requirements into manufacturable CAD designs, engineering calculations, design checks and drawing revisions. This is an anonymised professional experience case study, not a reconstruction of a client project.
approach: Produced preliminary AutoCAD layouts and SolidWorks part, assembly and manufacturing drawings.
Used EJMA-based engineering calculations and applicable ASME and project standards in bellows, material and piping-component design checks.
Reviewed guide-rod arrangements, bolted connections and flange thickness under operating-pressure and load considerations; used SolidWorks Simulation and ABAQUS for structural assessment.
Proposed material and thickness revisions to address corrosion concerns and supported selection of pipe and valve specifications for service conditions.
results: Examples of engineering decisions include material/thickness changes for corrosion mitigation and guide-rod quantity or flange thickness adjustments based on loads.
Work involved technical document reviews and coordination with fabrication teams.
limitations: Specific client drawings, confidential calculations, certified designs, numerical performance results and test data are not available for public release. Details are based on the engineer’s description of professional experience.
evidence: Employment experience described by the author; no confidential employer CAD assets reproduced.
engineering_question: How can expansion joints and connected piping components be sized and selected for pressure, displacement, corrosion exposure and fabrication requirements?
role: Mechanical Design Engineer at Enetaf Sane Co. I performed industrial design, technical review, load-related checks, materials work and drawing preparation. Employer and client drawings are intentionally not reproduced.
decisions: Translated operating-service requirements into bellows, expansion-joint, flange and piping-component configurations.
Reviewed guide-rod arrangement, bolt quantity and load paths, and revised flange thickness according to applied mechanical loads.
Selected or revised materials and wall thickness where corrosion exposure or specified service conditions required changes.
Assessed structural response in SolidWorks Simulation and ABAQUS; coordinated design feedback with fabrication colleagues.
verification: Engineering choices were checked with EJMA-based calculation software, applicable ASME / project requirements and structural calculations. No public numerical or certified design result is claimed.
reflection: The transferable skill is converting ambiguous service conditions into manufacturable geometry and defensible materials / load decisions. The public case is descriptive because the original drawings belong to the employer.

title: Buck Converter | Cascaded PI Control
subtitle: 100 V to 48 V, 1 kW converter design with current and voltage feedback loops
overview: Designed and documented a closed-loop DC–DC buck converter using an inner current loop and outer voltage loop, with an additional single-loop model for comparison. Component sizing and controller tuning were studied through steady-state, step-response and frequency-domain simulations.
approach: Sized the inductor and output capacitor around ripple requirements; compared single- and cascaded-loop structures.
Used MATLAB scripts and Simulink models to inspect gain crossover, phase margin, transient response and load variations.
Refined LC component values based on observed simulation behavior rather than relying on nominal sizing alone.
results: Nominal: 100 V input, 48 V output, 1 kW, 50 kHz switching.
Reported steady-state: 1.1% output-voltage ripple and 9.6% current ripple.
Full-load voltage step overshoot: 1.69%; no-load case: approximately 75% overshoot (important limitation).
limitations: No-load transient response is significantly underdamped in the supplied report. These are reported simulation results, not physical bench-test measurements.
evidence: 6-page report; single- and dual-loop Simulink models; MATLAB controller scripts; supporting component datasheets.
engineering_question: How can a 100 V-to-48 V converter maintain output regulation under load changes without excessive ripple or poorly damped transients?
role: I prepared the converter sizing calculations, single-loop and cascaded PI-controller designs, Simulink implementations and comparative evaluation.
decisions: Calculated nominal LC values from ripple design constraints, then iterated passive-component values using simulated load and step responses.
Implemented an inner inductor-current PI loop and an outer output-voltage PI loop; retained the single-loop model as a point of comparison.
Examined full-load and no-load Bode plots, controller phase margins, steady-state ripple and startup transient behavior.
Distinguished between outcomes that meet nominal specifications and the problematic lightly loaded response.
verification: Simulated nominal operating point: 100 V input, 48 V output, 1 kW, 50 kHz; reported voltage ripple ~1.1%, current ripple ~9.6%, full-load output overshoot 1.69%. No-load transient overshoot reached ~75%.
reflection: The no-load transient is a substantive limitation, not a success metric. Practical follow-up would address damping / light-load control and revalidate with switching and component nonidealities.

title: Inverted Pendulum | LQR & LQI
subtitle: Cart–pendulum stabilization, tracking, saturation and anti-windup
overview: Analysed the upright equilibrium of a cart–pendulum system and compared state-feedback pole placement with linear-quadratic regulator designs. Extended the study to integral tracking, actuator force constraints and nonlinear response.
approach: Derived and tested a state-space model; assessed reachability and open-loop instability.
Compared Ackermann pole placement against LQR based on transients and control effort.
Examined integral-action reference tracking, nonlinear attraction limits, saturation and anti-windup.
results: Demonstrated controller comparisons in report plots and MATLAB scripts.
Identified control-effort versus transient-response trade-offs and local validity of the linear model.
limitations: Academic simulations; the study does not demonstrate a physical stabilized pendulum.
evidence: 26-page CMS HW6 report and MATLAB implementation.
engineering_question: How should a controller stabilize an inherently unstable cart-pendulum equilibrium while respecting finite actuation?
role: I modelled and analysed the cart-pendulum dynamics, implemented controller comparisons, and evaluated tracking and saturation behavior in MATLAB/Simulink.
decisions: Linearized the system about the upright equilibrium and examined controllability and unstable pole locations.
Compared pole placement with optimal LQR state feedback, then introduced integral action for reference tracking.
Investigated nonlinear simulation, bounded control input, saturation and anti-windup implications.
verification: Controller-response plots and MATLAB/Simulink scripts show the comparative simulated dynamics and trade-offs. No physical cart-pendulum rig was tested.
reflection: Linear-controller performance is local to the selected equilibrium; nonlinear behavior and force saturation limit generalization.

title: Vehicle Cruise Control | PI & Anti-Windup
subtitle: Speed tracking under hills, actuator saturation and parameter changes
overview: Modelled a vehicle longitudinal plant, designed PI speed control, and explored road-grade disturbances, actuation limits, anti-windup and sensitivity functions.
approach: Implemented the nonlinear vehicle model and PI control simulations.
Introduced a road-grade disturbance and compared saturated controller behavior with and without anti-windup.
Assessed parameter sensitivity and gang-of-four frequency-domain plots.
results: Report comparison shows ~0.02 m/s peak overshoot with anti-windup versus ~0.885 m/s without it for one disturbance case.
limitations: Results are specific to simulated parameters and disturbance setup.
evidence: 37-page CMS HW4 part 1 report; MATLAB file, Simulink models and output figures.
engineering_question: How can a longitudinal vehicle-speed controller handle road grades and saturated throttle commands without excessive windup?
role: I wrote the modelling and control simulations, studied disturbances and anti-windup and analysed sensitivity/robustness in coursework.
decisions: Built a simplified longitudinal vehicle model and tuned PI speed regulation.
Introduced gradient disturbances and actuator saturation to challenge the nominal design.
Compared the transient under anti-windup and unmodified integral action; inspected sensitivity transfer functions.
verification: One reported disturbance scenario shows a peak speed overshoot near 0.02 m/s with anti-windup versus ~0.885 m/s without anti-windup. These figures are specific to that setup.
reflection: The study illustrates why actuator constraints must be included in controller assessment; it does not represent physical road testing.

title: Kalman Filtering | Penalty-Kick Tracking
subtitle: Tracking a moving target from noisy 2-D measurements
overview: Built a constant-velocity state-estimation model for a football penalty kick, then studied how a Kalman filter reduces position error under noisy measurements and uncertain initial velocities.
approach: Formulated a 2-D motion state and noisy measurement model.
Simulated ten variations of the kick initial state and velocity.
Evaluated estimation error at the target-reaching instant.
results: The supplied report states all ten simulated cases met its 0.25 m error criterion.
limitations: Simulation-only academic task; not a real camera-based ball tracking system.
evidence: 24-page CMS HW8 report with MATLAB code and simulation figures.
engineering_question: How can a noisy moving-target trajectory be estimated using a simple state-space motion model?
role: I implemented the simulated penalty-kick tracking model, Kalman estimator, numerical experiments and plotted evaluation.
decisions: Selected a constant-velocity state representation with explicit process and observation uncertainty.
Propagated state predictions and corrected them with noisy measured positions.
Compared estimated and reference trajectories across ten simulated initial-condition variants.
verification: The coursework report states that all ten simulated trials satisfied a 0.25 m endpoint tracking-error requirement.
reflection: This is a stochastic-estimation simulation, not camera tracking or field-tested real-time sensing. Model and noise assumptions determine filter quality.

title: Autonomous Obstacle-Avoiding Robot
subtitle: Arduino Uno, ultrasonic sensing, servo scanning and DC motor driving
overview: Built and programmed an Arduino-based obstacle-avoiding tracked mobile robot for an embedded-systems university assignment. The system integrates ultrasonic sensing, servo scanning, DC motor driving and threshold-based motion logic.
approach: Integrated Arduino Uno, HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, servo motor and dual DC geared motors.
Implemented repeated distance sampling with out-of-range filtering and averaging.
Used motor-control functions and threshold-based obstacle detection to stop, reverse and turn.
results: Report documents a 40 cm front obstacle threshold and timing-based drive commands.
Full Arduino source and a wiring diagram are present in the supplied group report.
limitations: The report describes choosing the clearer side, but the supplied final loop alternates turning with turnCounter. This inconsistency is disclosed rather than presenting unverified path planning.
evidence: Physical robot photograph supplied by the author; 15-page course report containing wiring and Arduino code. Original course report lists two participants.
engineering_question: Can a compact embedded controller detect obstacles and command a mobile platform using low-cost sensing and actuators?
role: I built, wired, programmed and tested the physical prototype, which was submitted as a two-person university group assignment. The photograph shows our actual hardware.
decisions: Integrated Arduino Uno, HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensing, an actuated scanning servo, L298N motor control and DC geared motors on a tracked platform.
Implemented ten-reading distance averaging with range filtering, then used a front-distance threshold to activate stop, reverse and turn functions.
Structured motor actions into reusable embedded functions and monitored sensed distances through serial output.
Used simple timed motion rather than localization, mapping or route planning, making behavior easier to reproduce and debug.
verification: The report supplies pin-level wiring and the full Arduino code; the uploaded photograph independently documents the assembled physical prototype. The implemented loop uses a 40 cm threshold.
reflection: The written description says the robot chooses the clearer side, but the final code alternates turn direction with a counter. The website therefore describes the code behavior rather than claiming a validated best-path planner.

title: Adaptive Cruise Control | PID vs Observer
subtitle: Distance-error regulation and disturbance estimation
overview: Studied adaptive cruise control as a following-distance regulation problem. Implemented and compared a PID approach against an observer-based feedback strategy to estimate unmeasured dynamics and disturbances.
approach: Formulated distance-error dynamics with leader acceleration and resistive disturbance terms.
Designed PID control and a state observer with performance targets from the coursework.
Compared time-domain responses and sensitivity measures.
results: The supplied report compares nominal simplicity of PID control with advantages of observer-based estimation.
limitations: Controller comparison is simulation-based; it is not a road-validated ADAS system.
evidence: 24-page CMS HW4 part 2 report, MATLAB code and comparison plots.
engineering_question: How should following-distance feedback be organized when lead-vehicle acceleration and disturbances are not directly measured?
role: I developed and compared PID-based and observer-based adaptive cruise control approaches using analytical models and MATLAB simulation.
decisions: Formulated the longitudinal distance-error dynamics with leader behaviour and disturbances.
Designed a conventional PID controller as an accessible reference strategy.
Evaluated a state-observer-based control formulation and compared tracking and robustness behavior.
verification: Coursework provides time-domain response figures for the controller alternatives and error trajectories; outputs are simulation-only.
reflection: The work is a model-based control comparison and does not establish ADAS safety validation or real-vehicle operation.

title: BMW 730 | Steering Dynamics
subtitle: Speed-dependent stability, damping and steering response
overview: Analysed a BMW 730 bicycle-model representation to understand speed-dependent lateral dynamics, controllability, observability, damping and steering response.
approach: Evaluated eigenvalues, transfer functions and speed-dependent dynamic properties.
Compared understeering / oversteering conditions using zero-frequency gains.
Designed feedback for selected lateral or yaw-rate response objectives.
results: The report documents a damping-ratio improvement in a selected closed-loop case (approximately 0.088 to 0.628).
limitations: Based on an academic vehicle model, not measurement of a production BMW vehicle.
evidence: 38-page CMS HW5 part 1 report and supporting MATLAB code.
engineering_question: How do vehicle forward speed and model parameters change lateral stability and steering-response behavior?
role: I analysed the specified BMW 730 bicycle-model problem, assessed dynamic properties and implemented feedback studies in MATLAB.
decisions: Computed speed-dependent poles/eigenvalues and transfer-function responses for the academic lateral vehicle model.
Studied controllability, observability and understeer/oversteer tendencies.
Analysed the influence of feedback design on damping and transient response.
verification: The report shows a selected damping-ratio change from roughly 0.088 to 0.628 under its model and controller assumptions.
reflection: BMW appears as the reference vehicle in an academic model; this is not BMW production-system engineering or measurements.

title: Active Steering | Observer & Wiener Filter
subtitle: PI feedback versus observer-based yaw-rate regulation
overview: Extended the BMW 730 steering model into controller and state-estimator comparisons. Investigated PI pole placement, Luenberger observer design and a Wiener-filter-inspired observer under uncertainty and noise.
approach: Designed a PI controller using characteristic-polynomial constraints.
Compared deterministic state observation with covariance-weighted Wiener estimation.
Examined speed-dependent tracking and stability through time- and frequency-domain results.
results: The report analyses state-estimation quality and trade-offs between controller complexity and measurement noise sensitivity.
limitations: Filter performance depends on assumed process and measurement covariance.
evidence: 38-page CMS HW5 part 2 report and MATLAB analysis script.
engineering_question: Can active steering regulation and state estimation remain useful when lateral vehicle dynamics are uncertain or noisy?
role: I developed steering-controller and observer comparisons, including PI feedback, Luenberger observation and covariance-weighted estimation.
decisions: Built a closed-loop yaw-rate/steering formulation from the selected vehicle model.
Derived PI-controller parameters with characteristic-equation objectives.
Compared deterministic observer behavior with Wiener/Kalman-like covariance-weighted estimation assumptions.
verification: The supplied report includes observer/controller diagrams and sensitivity plots; no numerical road-test claim is made.
reflection: Performance depends strongly on assumed noise statistics, model structure and vehicle operating speed.

title: Bicycle Roll | Stability & Feedback
subtitle: Speed-dependent roll dynamics and feedback stabilization
overview: Examined simplified roll dynamics and a Whipple-model bicycle representation, exploring why stability and steering authority change with forward speed.
approach: Derived steering-to-roll transfer functions and investigated poles, zeros and gain.
Compared proportional stabilization and more capable feedback designs.
Evaluated speed-dependent stability and limitations near low forward speed.
results: The report highlights sensitivity of stabilization to model order, speed and sensing assumptions.
limitations: Academic model study; no physical autonomous bicycle test is documented.
evidence: 26-page CMS HW7 report with MATLAB analysis.
engineering_question: Why does balancing performance change with forward speed, and what type of feedback can regulate bicycle roll?
role: I modelled bicycle roll/steering dynamics, tested stability assumptions and studied candidate feedback controllers in MATLAB.
decisions: Used simplified roll equations and a Whipple-type bicycle model to study a balance-control problem.
Inspected poles, zeros and steering-to-roll dynamics at different speeds.
Compared the behaviour of elementary proportional control with more structured feedback.
verification: The report documents transfer functions, stability plots and controller comparisons under the adopted academic model assumptions.
reflection: The simplified models are sensitive to speed and sensor/actuation assumptions. No physical robotic bicycle prototype was built.

title: EV / HEV Traffic Co-Simulation | Rome
subtitle: SUMO traffic + Python bridge + MATLAB/Simulink vehicle models
overview: Built a Rome urban-traffic simulation workflow using SUMO route data and Python interfaces linked with MATLAB/Simulink EV and HEV models. The project contains multiple traffic intensities, vehicle-model files and saved scenario results.
approach: Prepared light, medium and heavy traffic scenarios with SUMO-compatible routes.
Connected traffic speed traces and vehicle simulation via Python/MATLAB bridging scripts.
Compared speed tracking, state-of-charge trends and energy/fuel-equivalent outputs across scenarios.
results: Archived CSV summaries contain light, medium and heavy scenarios and actual-versus-reference speed records.
Separate EV and HEV Simulink models and scenario plots are included.
limitations: Saved scenario results have not been independently rerun in the current environment; do not interpret equivalent-fuel quantities as laboratory vehicle measurements.
evidence: Project RAR contains Python scripts, MATLAB bridges, .slx models, route files, result CSVs and figures.
engineering_question: How can urban traffic demand be connected to electric and hybrid vehicle model simulations to compare speed tracking and energy use?
role: I prepared the SUMO urban-route simulation, Python-to-MATLAB/Simulink interface and archived EV/HEV scenario outputs.
decisions: Defined different urban traffic intensities and exported driving profiles from SUMO scenarios.
Linked speed profiles to EV and HEV dynamic models through Python and MATLAB/Simulink scripts.
Compared reference versus simulated speed, battery charge trends and model energy outputs over traffic cases.
verification: The supplied archive contains SUMO inputs, Python scripts, Simulink model files, scenario CSV tables and plotted results. Archived outputs were inspected but not rerun.
reflection: Reported energy/fuel-equivalent figures are model outputs and should not be interpreted as real-vehicle fuel measurements or independently validated emissions.

title: Fusion 360 | CAD/CAM CNC Workflow
subtitle: Aluminium 6061 milling plan with machining simulation and NC output
overview: Prepared a Fusion 360 CAD/CAM course challenge for an aluminium 6061 workpiece, setting up machining coordinates and tooling, then creating and validating a multi-operation 2-D milling workflow.
approach: Defined stock, tool library, work coordinate origin and milling setup.
Created Face, Adaptive Clearing, Pocket, Contour and drilling toolpaths.
Simulated material removal and exported an NC program using a generic post.
results: The course summary confirms simulated stock removal and NC export; the Fusion design archive (.f3d) is available.
limitations: A CAM simulation and generic NC post do not establish physical machining quality or actual machine validation.
evidence: Fusion .f3d file plus one-page process report.
engineering_question: How can a parametrically modelled aluminium part be translated into a verifiable two-dimensional CNC machining workflow?

Defined setup direction, work coordinate origin and stock definition to align programming with the intended fixture orientation.
Sequenced Face, 2D Adaptive, Pocket, Contour and Drill operations rather than relying on one generic toolpath.
Simulated material removal and used a generic 2D post-processor to export an NC file.

title: Moss Detection | Classical Vision & DeepLabv3+
subtitle: Hybrid active contour compared with DeepLabv3+ ResNet-50
overview: Designed and evaluated wall-surface moss segmentation using a classical image-processing pipeline and a DeepLabv3+ (ResNet-50) semantic segmentation system. Submitted as a two-person academic presentation; the implementation and evaluation were carried out by the portfolio author.
approach: Implemented/reported a direct MATLAB image-processing sequence: green-channel enhancement, CLAHE, median filtering, Canny edges, morphological operations and active-contour refinement.
Evaluated a DeepLabv3+ semantic-segmentation workflow with ResNet-50, labeled masks, data augmentation, weighted classification and post-processing.
Compared representative predictions and train/test F-measure distributions; documented false-positive and under-segmentation cases.
results: Presentation reports direct-method averages: CR (precision) 0.833, CM (recall) 0.902 and F-measure 0.831.
Deep-learning predictions are illustrated with best/worst cases and train/test box plots; a single verified numerical aggregate for this method was not available.
Project includes MATLAB source snippets and a 14-slide two-author project presentation.
limitations: Academic group project. Classical method may over-segment textured backgrounds; deep learning can under-segment low-contrast moss. The supplied slide deck cites 25 training epochs, whereas shared code variants specify different settings; an independently reproduced training run has not been verified.
evidence: July 2025 two-person course presentation, MATLAB DeepLabv3+ scripts and segmentation-evaluation material. Author states responsibility for implementation.
engineering_question: Which method segments moss on textured walls more reliably: classical image processing or a learned pixel-level segmentation network?
role: I developed the MATLAB processing and segmentation workflows, compared predictions and documented results for a project submitted with a second named course participant.
decisions: Implemented a classical pipeline involving green-channel enhancement, CLAHE, median filtering, Canny detection, morphology and Chan–Vese active contour.
Implemented and evaluated DeepLabv3+ with a ResNet-50 backbone, data augmentation, labeled segmentation masks and class weighting.
Reviewed best/worst image predictions and precision, recall, F-measure and area-ratio distributions.
verification: The presentation reports for the classical pipeline precision (CR) 0.833, recall (CM) 0.902 and F-measure 0.831. Deep-learning train/test distributions are plotted but no independently reproduced global benchmark is available.
reflection: Classical segmentation over-detects textured regions; deep learning can under-detect difficult vegetation. MATLAB code fragments and slides use differing training-epoch settings, so runtime reproducibility needs a consolidated script and dataset documentation.
